title: Evaluation under one rational-component contraction
statement: Let $T$ be any scheme [def-pc-scheme]. Let $(Y\to T,t_1,\ldots,t_r,t)$ and $(X\to T,s_1,\ldots,s_r)$ be stable ordered pointed families of genus $g\geq2$, with the conventions of [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids] and [def-sfb-stable-pointed-curve]. Suppose $q:Y\to X$ is a $T$-morphism with $q t_i=s_i$ and put $\Delta=q t$. Assume each geometric fibre of $q$ is either an isomorphism or contracts just one smooth rational component containing $t$ and having exactly three special points when $t$ is counted, and is an isomorphism elsewhere; the special points mean the branches of nodes and all markings on the normalized component. Put $D=\sum s_i(T)$, $E=\sum t_i(T)$, $\mathcal J=\ker(\mathcal O_X\to\Delta_*\mathcal O_T)$ and $\mathcal K=\operatorname{coker}(\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{(1,1)}\mathcal J^\vee\oplus\mathcal O_X(D))$, where $\mathcal J^\vee=\mathcal Hom(\mathcal J,\mathcal O_X)$ and the maps are multiplication and the divisor inclusion. Divisor modules use [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle]. There are canonical identifications $q_*\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_X$, $q_*\mathcal O_Y(-E)=\mathcal O_X(-D)$, $q_*\mathcal O_Y(t-E)=\mathcal J^\vee\otimes\mathcal O_X(-D)$ and $q_*\mathcal O_Y(t)=\mathcal K\otimes\mathcal O_X(-D)$. Under the last identification, evaluation is a surjection $q^*(\mathcal K\otimes\mathcal O_X(-D))\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y(t)$. Equivalently it is an invertible quotient $q^*\mathcal K\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y(t)\otimes q^*\mathcal O_X(D)$. The corresponding map $Y\to\operatorname{Proj}_X(\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal K)$, interpreted by the invertible-quotient convention [lem-trf-projective-bundle-quotient-geometry], sends the ordered sections to the quotient lifts from the two summands. On geometric fibres it is the identity off the exceptional component and identifies that component with the exceptional projective line by its complete degree-one linear system; in the isomorphism case it is an isomorphism on the entire fibre. The identifications and quotient maps commute with arbitrary base change and with every isomorphism of contraction diagrams, including automorphisms over the identity of $X$.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed pp.178--179), using Section 1, Corollary 1.5 and Lemma 1.6: multiplication and the pushforward exact sequences, retaining the twist by minus the old-marking divisor. Local PDF WANTED; primary-author scan consulted online.

proof.text: The stable-family definitions give proper, flat finitely presented nodal families; projectivity implies properness, and properness of $Y/T$ with separatedness of $X/T$ makes $q$ proper. Work on a geometric fibre. The branch lemma identifies the complement's normalized branches with those of $X$ at $x=q(A)$, so $A$ has one or two attachments, all transverse and distinct. Its other old special points are old markings. Since it has three special points including $t$, the possibilities are a tail with one attachment and exactly one $t_i$, or a bridge with two attachments and no $t_i$. The tail image is smooth and equals $s_i$; the bridge image is a node. The same branch lemma identifies the remaining curve with $X$ in the tail case and with its partial normalization at $x$ in the bridge case. The exceptional component cannot be the whole connected fibre, because its genus would be zero instead of $g\geq2$.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: Set $F_0=\mathcal O_Y$, $F_E=\mathcal O_Y(-E)$, $F_{-t}=\mathcal O_Y(-t)$, $F_N=\mathcal O_Y(t-E)$ and $F_t=\mathcal O_Y(t)$. Each marked section lies in the relative smooth locus. Restrict the curve to that open locus and apply the smooth-curve-section Cartier lemma; properness makes the sections closed in the full curve, so being Cartier near their images and having unit ideal elsewhere proves they are Cartier on the full curve. Thus these are invertible divisor modules. If $m$ is the number of old markings on a contracted component, then $m\in\{0,1\}$ and their exceptional degrees are respectively $0,-m,-1,1-m,1$. Apply the line-cohomology lemma to each: all five direct images are finitely presented and $T$-flat, all first higher direct images vanish, and their formation commutes with every base change on $T$. For $F_t$ the exceptional degree is one, so evaluation $q^*q_*F_t\twoheadrightarrow F_t$ is surjective. The degree condition is vacuous on isomorphism fibres. Apply the dual-section-ideal lemma to $(X/T,\Delta)$: $\mathcal J^\vee(-D)$ is also finitely presented and $T$-flat and commutes with base change (locally the divisor factor is free of rank one).

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: There are natural maps $\alpha:\mathcal O_X\to q_*F_0$ and $\beta:\mathcal O_X(-D)\to q_*F_E$: pull back a function, respectively a function vanishing on all $s_i$; it then vanishes on all $t_i$. Check them on geometric fibres, using the closed-union ring identity to describe functions as functions on the remaining curve and on $A$ with equal attachment values. For $F_0$, a function on $A\simeq\mathbf P^1$ is constant. At a tail this is determined by its one boundary value; at a bridge the two branch values must agree. These are exactly functions on $X$. For $F_E$, a tail has $F_E|_A=\mathcal O(-1)$ and thus no section on $A$; the remaining function must vanish at the attachment, giving $\mathcal O_X(-s_i)$ there. At a bridge $E$ avoids $A$, so the same equal-value rule as for $F_0$ applies. Away from the exceptional image the assertion is the given isomorphism and the same old divisor; in the isomorphism case it is tautological. Here the polynomial descriptions $H^0(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O)=\Omega$ and $H^0(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ follow by writing sections on its two affine charts and matching on their overlap.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: The fibre identifications make $\alpha,\beta$ isomorphisms over $T$. Explicitly, at $x\in X$ over $a\in T$, Nakayama applied to the finite cokernel first gives surjectivity from surjectivity on the geometric fibre (field extension is faithful). The target is flat over $\mathcal O_{T,a}$ by step 2. Tensoring a surjection onto a flat module therefore preserves its kernel sequence, so the kernel has zero fibre. This kernel is finite: choose finitely many source generators; the target's finite presentation makes the relations among their images finitely generated, and their image generates the kernel. Nakayama now kills the kernel. Thus $q_*F_0=\mathcal O_X$ and $q_*F_E=\mathcal O_X(-D)$ through these actual maps. The same argument will apply to the comparison in step 7, whose target is $T$-flat by step 2. Left exactness of direct image applied to $0\to F_{-t}\to F_0\to t_*\mathcal O_T\to0$ identifies $q_*F_{-t}$ with $\ker(\mathcal O_X\to\Delta_*\mathcal O_T)=\mathcal J$; kernels are computed sectionwise, and $q t=\Delta$.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: Multiplication of divisor modules gives $F_{-t}\otimes F_N\to F_E$. With step 4 it defines a canonical map $\mu:q_*F_N\to\mathcal Hom(\mathcal J,\mathcal O_X(-D))=\mathcal J^\vee\otimes\mathcal O_X(-D)$ by $b\mapsto(a\mapsto ab)$. The equality on the right is checked after locally trivializing $\mathcal O_X(-D)$. This map uses the already constructed identification $q_*F_{-t}=\mathcal J$, rather than presuming that pulling back $\mathcal J$ is invertible. Away from the exceptional image, and on an isomorphism fibre, it is the multiplication isomorphism for the Cartier divisor $t$.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: For a geometric tail, write $x=s_i=\Delta$. The remaining curve is $X$, while $F_N|_A=\mathcal O_A(t-t_i)$ is trivial: choose a rational coordinate with zero at $t_i$ and pole at $t$, whose divisor is $t_i-t$. A section on $A$ is determined by its boundary value at the attachment, since that point is disjoint from $t,t_i$. Thus forgetting the exceptional section identifies $q_*F_N$ locally at $x$ with $\mathcal O_X$ through its remaining-curve value. On $X$, $\mathcal J=\mathcal O_X(-x)$ and locally $D=x$. Multiplication takes that remaining-curve value $b$ to the homomorphism $a\mapsto ab$ from $\mathcal O_X(-x)$ to itself. This is exactly the isomorphism $\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal J^\vee(-D)$. All other old markings are disjoint from $x$ and contribute the same invertible factor on both sides. Hence $\mu$ is an isomorphism on every tail fibre.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: For a geometric bridge, $E$ avoids $A$, and $F_N|_A=\mathcal O_A(t)$. A section of this line is uniquely determined by its values at the two attachment points: choose their coordinates $0,\infty$, so sections have the form $aU+bV$ and the two values give $b,a$. Consequently the closed-union description identifies $q_*F_N$ with $\nu_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde X}$ near $x$, where $\nu$ separates the two branches of $X$ at $x$. The dual-section-ideal lemma identifies $\mathcal J^\vee$ with precisely this multiplier module, and $D$ avoids $x$. Under these identifications, multiplication sends a branch function $b$ to $a\mapsto ab$, so $\mu$ is the identity of this module. Combining with steps 5--6 proves it is an isomorphism on every geometric fibre. Apply the finite-kernel/Nakayama argument of step 4, using step 2's flat target, to obtain $q_*\mathcal O_Y(t-E)\cong\mathcal J^\vee(-D)$ on $X$.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: The disjoint Cartier divisors $t$ and $E$ give the exact sequence $0\to F_E\xrightarrow{(1,1)}F_N\oplus F_0\xrightarrow{(b,c)\mapsto b-c}F_t\to0$. Check it off $t\cup E$, near $t$ where $E$ is empty, and near $E$ where $t$ is empty: one of the two summand inclusions is then an isomorphism, the difference is surjective, and its kernel is the displayed diagonal. The direct-image long exact sequence and $R^1q_*F_E=0$ from step 2 make its pushforward short exact. Module sheaves have enough injectives, so the right-derived delta-functor applies to the left exact direct image. Using steps 4 and 7, its first arrow is $\mathcal O_X(-D)\to\mathcal J^\vee(-D)\oplus\mathcal O_X$, with components multiplication and the divisor inclusion: on the first component the image of $f$ acts on $a\in\mathcal J$ as $a\mapsto af$. This is the defining sequence of $\mathcal K$ tensored by $\mathcal O_X(-D)$, so its cokernel is $\mathcal K(-D)$. Thus the induced cokernel isomorphism is $q_*F_t\cong\mathcal K(-D)$, retaining the negative $D$ twist.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: Transport step 2's surjective evaluation along the cokernel isomorphism and tensor with the invertible module $q^*\mathcal O_X(D)$. This gives $q^*\mathcal K\twoheadrightarrow F_t\otimes q^*\mathcal O_X(D)$. The quotient-geometry theorem attaches the required $X$-map into $\operatorname{Proj}_X(\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal K)$. At each old section $t_i$, the $F_N$ inclusion in $F_t$ vanishes because of the factor $-E$; hence the quotient factors through the cokernel of the $\mathcal J^\vee$ summand. At $t$, the $F_0$ inclusion in $F_t$ vanishes, so it factors through the cokernel of the $\mathcal O_X(D)$ summand. The expansion lemma states that these are the invertible quotients defining the ordered lifts. Factorization of the surjective quotient through these lines gives exactly those quotient classes, including the harmless sign in $b-c$. Thus every old label and the last label is sent to its prescribed lift.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: On a geometric fibre the expansion lemma identifies the target with $X$ off the exceptional image. The constructed map is over $X$, hence is the identity on that open. On $A$, $q^*\mathcal O_X(D)$ is a constant line, so the quotient line has degree one. The evaluation supplies its complete two-dimensional space of sections: on a bridge the two attachment values are independent by step 7; on a tail any section of $\mathcal O_A(t)$ extends near the exceptional image, since its one boundary value is matched by a regular function on the remaining curve. The closed-union description gives these extensions explicitly. In coordinates a basis gives $[U:V]\mapsto[U:V]$, after changing bases by an invertible matrix. Thus $A$ identifies with the target's exceptional projective line by its complete degree-one system. On an isomorphism fibre, $\Delta$ is smooth and disjoint from $D$; the expansion lemma says the target is $X$ itself, so the map over $X$ is an isomorphism of the entire fibre.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).

proof.text: Every comparison just used is a specified map: pullback of functions for $\alpha,\beta$, a kernel for $\mathcal J$, multiplication for $\mu$, the diagonal and difference for the exact sequence, its induced cokernel map, and adjunction evaluation for the quotient. Direct-image base change for the five modules is supplied by the line-cohomology lemma; base change of the dual and its multiplication inclusion is supplied by the dual-section-ideal lemma. Cartier divisor ideals and their inclusions pull back for these smooth disjoint sections. These facts carry the defining maps to the same maps after every $T'\to T$, and therefore carry their inverse isomorphisms and the cokernel identification to the corresponding ones. The expansion lemma and quotient-geometry theorem give the same compatibility for the target and its lifts. For an isomorphism of contraction diagrams all function pullbacks and multiplication squares commute, the section ideals are carried to the same ideals, and the difference map remains $(b,c)\mapsto b-c$. Adjunction evaluation is natural, so the resulting quotient classes agree. Naturality of the quotient classification then makes the $X$-maps agree. This also applies to automorphisms over $1_X$; no choice of a coordinate on $A$ entered any construction.

source.place: Section 2, Lemma 2.5 (printed p.178), with Section 1, Corollary 1.5 (p.167).
